title: Theoretical Neurobiology Group
subtitle: Weekly research seminars on active inference and the free energy principle.
audience: Researchers and learners in neuroscience, mathematics, machine learning, psychology, philosophy, medicine, and biology.
lede: Founded by Prof. Karl Friston, the Theoretical Neurobiology (TNB) Group advances research on active inference and the free energy principle through interdisciplinary talks and discussion.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.body: The group has fostered interdisciplinary collaboration for decades. Its meetings bring together empirical data and analysis, simulations, and mathematical work on active inference and the free energy principle.

sections.heading: Meeting Details
sections.body: Meetings take place every Tuesday at 2:30 pm UK time on Zoom and last about two hours. A typical session includes a 40-minute presentation, 40 minutes of questions and answers, and 40 minutes of discussion and feedback with Prof. Friston.

sections.heading: How to Participate
sections.body: To join the mailing list and receive the Zoom link, email the group with a brief introduction. Include what you work on and how you are connected to the field. The group welcomes contributions from a wide range of disciplines.

sections.heading: Recordings
sections.body: The TNB YouTube playlists organise past meetings by research area.

sections.heading: Chair — Samuel William Nehrer
sections.body:
Samuel is a Master's student at the Institute of Neuroinformatics, a joint institute of ETH Zürich and the University of Zürich. He completed his undergraduate studies in Cognitive Science at Aarhus University, where he began developing Julia implementations of active inference models for cognitive modelling.

He is interested in combining computational modelling of human behaviour with brain imaging to address how psychedelics modulate hierarchical inference, cognitive flexibility, and belief updating at the algorithmic level, and how the ensuing computations are implemented in brain networks. He is also an aviation enthusiast and enjoys thinking about fundamental questions in physics and the philosophy of mind, as well as exploring the Swiss mountains on foot or by bike.

sections.heading: Chair — Peter Thestrup Waade
sections.body:
Peter's research focuses on computational cognitive modelling of multi-scale social interaction, particularly from the perspective of active inference and predictive processing. He did his PhD with Chris Mathys at the Interacting Minds Centre at Aarhus University and is starting a postdoc at the Translational Neuromodeling Unit at ETH Zürich with Klaas Stephan.

He develops Julia software for cognitive modelling in general, the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter, and active inference with POMDPs, and also works in consciousness research, on joint action in partner dancing, and on Chinese philosophy and predictive processing.

sections.heading: Chair — Robert Chis-Ciure, PhD
sections.body:
Robert is an ERC postdoctoral research fellow in Anil Seth's lab at the University of Sussex and the Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science. His research focuses on formalised notions of emergence and computational neurophenomenology, using hybrid predictive coding and active inference formalisms to model phenomenal properties of experience and validate them experimentally — building toward a new methodological paradigm, Phenomenomics, to characterise the inner worlds of human and eventually all other observers, including by leveraging AI/ML on large-scale datasets.

Before Sussex he was a Fulbright postdoc at NYU under David Chalmers, a Tatiana Foundation postdoc in Georg Northoff's lab, and worked in Giulio Tononi's lab on consciousness at the intersection of philosophy, neuroscience, and computational modelling. He is also an affiliated researcher at the Wolfram Institute.

sections.heading: Chair — Will Yun-Farmbrough
sections.body:
Will is a PhD student at the Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science, supervised by Anil Seth and Chris Buckley. His research investigates how perceptual phenomenology in human subjects can constrain and inform predictive coding models of cortical processing — the algorithmic underpinnings for how our world appears to us.

He is also interested in predictive processing approaches to the meta-problem of consciousness, seeking to understand how intuitions of conscious experience and qualia might arise naturally in certain generative model hierarchies. He enjoys surfing, houseplants, and zen.

sections.heading: Chair — Jonathan Ehrenreich Laursen
sections.body:
Jonathan is a Master's student in Neural Systems and Computation at ETH Zürich and the University of Zürich, where he works on developing cognitive modelling software in Julia. He is interested in using computational tools to understand psychiatric disorders and how they might become relevant for clinical practice.

Beyond his studies, he is an avid reader of history and philosophy and enjoys spending time outdoors.

sections.heading: Chair — Dominik Firisz
sections.body:
Dominik studies cognitive science at Aarhus University in Denmark and is completing a thesis in computational psychiatry at the Translational Neuromodeling Unit in Zürich. He plans to spend his final semester at Waseda University in Tokyo studying mathematical approaches to the neural and computational mechanisms of psychiatric conditions.

His research interests include combining neuroimaging and computational modelling to study psychopathology. Outside his studies, he enjoys philosophy of mind, science fiction, thrillers, and challenging video games.

sections.heading: Work in Progress
sections.body: The group is compiling an active inference resource collection with introductory material, research papers, and tutorials. It is also planning joint research symposia with other communities to build cross-disciplinary collaboration.
